title: GHz non-reciprocal optical conductivity in hematite ($α$-$\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3$)
authors: Peng Rao, Johannes Gröbmeyer, P. Peter Stavropoulos, Alexander Mook, Matthias Althammer, Hans Huebl, Alexander Holleitner, Johannes Knolle
abstract: We study the non-reciprocal properties of the iron oxide $α$-Fe$_2$O$_3$ (hematite) in the canted easy-plane antiferromagnetic phase, specifically in the GHz to THz frequency range. First, using the the microscopic spin Hamiltonian, we obtain the correct classical ground state where the canting is induced by the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMI). The magnon spectrum is simulated using linear spin wave theory. We then compute the polarizability and the sub-gap optical conductivities using linear response. We find that the conductivity tensor contains frequency peaks at the zero momentum magnon gaps of order $0.1~$meV which can be tuned by the DMI and on-site anisotropic spin interactions. Furthermore, we show that the canting-induced net magnetic moment $\mathbf{m}$ represents a measure for the effective time-reversal-symmetry breaking and non-reciprocity of the system: a finite $\mathbf{m}$ results in a non-zero Hall conductivity. Finally, we discuss the prospective application of hematite in non-reciprocal circulator design, by computing the non-reciprocal circulator transmission amplitude using the conductivities as input.
summary: The paper theoretically investigates how Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions induce a net magnetization in hematite ($\alpha$-Fe$_2$O$_3$), leading to non-reciprocal optical conductivity. By calculating the anomalous Hall conductivity using magnon theory, the authors demonstrate that this material can be engineered for use in high-frequency non-reciprocal circulators.
main_problem: The study investigates non-reciprocal optical conductivity in hematite ($\alpha$-Fe$_2$O$_3$) within the GHz to THz frequency range.
main_result: The finite net magnetic moment, induced by Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions (DMI), leads to a non-zero anomalous Hall conductivity and allows for the design of non-reciprocal circulators.
method: Linear response theory is used with Kubo's formula applied to single-magnon contributions derived from linear spin wave theory analysis of the magnetic Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The system is hematite ($\alpha$-Fe$_2$O$_3$), modeled as a canted easy-plane antiferromagnet. The physics is governed by a spin Hamiltonian including exchange, DMI, and anisotropy terms.
key_observables: Non-reciprocal optical conductivity tensor components ($\sigma_{xy}$), anomalous Hall conductivity ($\sigma^{(as)}$), and circulator transmission amplitude ($|S_{13}|/|S_{31}|$)
important_parameters: DMI energy scale ($\sim 0.1 	ext{ meV}$); magnetic anisotropy terms ($d_2, d_6$); operating frequency range (GHz to THz).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the single-magnon approximation for conductivity and treats the system in the weak ferromagnetic phase above $T_M$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the magnon spectrum near $\Gamma$, the dependence of magnon gaps on anisotropy, and simulated non-reciprocal responses $|S_{13}|/|S_{31}|$ vs. frequency for a circulator.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the magnetic ground state via spin Hamiltonian analysis to calculating the optical conductivity using linear response theory, culminating in the application of these results to model a three-port non-reciprocal circulator.
why_interesting: This work connects fundamental magnetism (DMI, canting) directly to macroscopic quantum phenomena like non-reciprocity and device physics (circulators), which is highly relevant for understanding spin-charge coupling in magnetic insulators.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Illustration of the unit cell of hematite (α −Fe2O3), showing iron atoms in brown and oxygen atoms in red. (a) Side-view of the unit cell with the magnetic moments shown in blue. (b) Top view looking down the c-axis. The in-plane projection of the lattice and the vectors a1, a2 and a3 are shown. The magnetic moments M1 (sub- lattices A, D) and M2 (sublattices B,C) are almost anti-parallel and in-plane.

FIG. 2. Linear spin wave spectrum for the spin Hamiltonian Eq. (1). (a) Magnon spectrum across the Brillouin zone (BZ) of αFe2O3. Here, four magnon branches are pair-wise almost degenerate (ma- genta and purple lines for each pair). (b) The magnon spectrum near the Γ-point. The lower magnon branch corresponds to in-plane os- cillations of the Ne´el vector and the higher branch to out-of-plane oscillations.

FIG. 3. Minimal magnon gaps energy of the two lower branches in Fig. 2(b) as a function of the triaxial basal anisotropy strength d6 in Eq. (6). The gray dashed line corresponds to d6 = 10−8 meV used elsewhere in the paper. Only the blue branch depends on d6 since it corresponds to in-plane oscillations. The strong dependence on d6 is due to the exchange enhancement effect discussed below Eq. (8).

FIG. 4. Real part of conductivities of the spin Hamiltonian Eq. (1) as a function of frequency ω. (a) Longitudinal conductivities where Re σxx and Re σyy couple to the lower and higher magnon branches in Fig. (2)(b) respectively. (b) The non-zero antisymmetric conduc- tivity component satisfying Eq. (22), coupling to the higher magnon branch. The other off-diagonal conductivities are zero.

FIG. 5. Scheme of a three-port circulator with the sample material in the center. The circulator ports 1, 2, and 3 are capacitively coupled via Cedge to the sample (hematite). The term Cp describes the para- sitic coupling between the port arms.

Spintronics.note: The paper directly investigates non-reciprocal optical conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$) in a magnetic insulator ($\alpha$-Fe$_2$O$_3$) using magnon theory, which falls squarely into the quantum-optics/spintronics interface concerning spin transport and magnet-optical response.
